extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of classical essays, philosophy, and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading or translation/annotation of Michel de Montaigne's essays (classical Renaissance personal essays), with attention to his rhetorical choices, moral prescriptions, and examples. Useful for literary scholars, translators, and reflective writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodate subject to one's strength
rubrics_metrics.description: I have accommodated my subject to my strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explains he avoids continuous narrative and does not force himself into forms beyond his natural capacity: he interrupts and cuts himself short for want of breath, declines assiduity or perseverance, and will not imitate a guide if he cannot keep pace. As writing advice: choose subjects and forms that fit your natural abilities; avoid overreaching stylistically or pretending expertise you do not have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in reporting examples
rubrics_metrics.description: In the examples which I here bring in, of what I have heard, read, done, or said, I have forbidden myself to dare to alter even the most light and indifferent circumstances; my conscience does not falsify one tittle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne sets a norm of not falsifying even minor details when presenting anecdotes or historical examples. For writers and historians: avoid inventing or altering particulars; preserve the truthfulness of reported incidents even when they serve illustrative purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer writing of the past over the present
rubrics_metrics.description: I think it less hazardous to write of things past, than present, by how much the writer is only to give an account of things every one knows he must of necessity borrow upon trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that writing about contemporary affairs risks staking reputation on popular or partisan opinions and on unknown intentions. As a guideline: be cautious about composing authoritative accounts of current events or passing judgments about living persons or factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of similitudes/fabricated examples is a licensed rhetorical device (but use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a just liberty allowed in the schools, of supposing similitudes, when they have none at hand. I do not, however, make any use of that privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical rhetorical practice permits inventing analogies or hypothetical examples to illustrate points, but Montaigne states he refrains from this privilege. Guidance for writers: rhetorical invention is acceptable in some genres, but if you choose to use it, be mindful about signalling it and not passing fiction as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate children to abhor vices from the start
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should carefully be instructed to abhor vices for their own contexture; and the natural deformity of those vices ought so to be represented to them, that the very thought should be hateful to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne treats children's play as serious moral formation: small dishonesties in games seed larger adult vices. As an educational norm: instill aversion to deceit and cruelty early, portray the true deformity of vices, and treat childhood actions as formative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware custom's stupefying power on senses and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom is a violent and treacherous schoolmistress... continually being accustomed to anything, blinds the eye of our judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne illustrates how repeated exposure makes extreme or strange things seem normal (noise, diet, rituals). For critical thinking: actively question habitual beliefs and sensations; recognize how acclimation can deaden sensitivity and distort judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ethnocentric or reflexive judgments of other customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Barbarians are no more a wonder to us, than we are to them... if after having travelled over those remote examples, men could settle themselves to reflect upon, and rightly to confer them, with their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating foreign practices, do not dismiss them as absurd merely from unfamiliarity. Montaigne recommends reflective comparison rather than ethnocentric astonishment. For cultural critique: practice reciprocal perspective-taking and avoid facile moral superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept testimony from minds prepossessed by custom when seeking truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it not a shame for a natural philosopher... to seek testimony of the truth from minds prepossessed by custom?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Cicero, Montaigne warns that witnesses or observers shaped by entrenched custom are unreliable evidence for natural truth. For empirical or philosophical inquiry: prefer observations and testimony less tainted by habitual bias; account for cultural conditioning when using testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is acceptable to use memorable or even fabulous examples if they are within human possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Amongst the various readings thereof in history, I cull out the most rare and memorable to fit my own turn. There are authors whose only end and design it is to give an account of things that have happened; mine, if I could arrive unto it, should be to deliver of what may happen... whether they have really happened or no, 'tis still within the verge of human capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne defends selecting striking anecdotes (even questionable ones) if they serve to illuminate human behavior or possibility. For essayists: illustrative examples—true, probable, or plausible—can be rhetorically effective, but distinguish their status (reported fact vs. possibility) and use them to clarify human tendencies rather than to mislead.
